text: How a 1998 engine drew a frame.
In the 1990s, Argonaut Software licensed a real-time 3D engine called BRender.
Games such as Carmageddon and Croc were built on it.
In 2022 a 1998 version of its source was published under the MIT licence, with the approval of Argonaut's former chief executive, Jez San.
To rebuild it, we did not try to run a whole game first.
We built a ladder: twenty-one small programs, each proving one step a frame depends on.
If a rung fails, you know which step broke.
Which step do you think breaks first on a modern computer?
The first rungs are plain maths: vectors, the engine starting and stopping, and a perspective matrix that turns 3D points into 2D ones.
Join the points and you have a wireframe cube.
Hang models on a scene graph and the engine moves them as one.
Next the ladder fills each triangle a row of pixels at a time, lighting each face by how much it faces the light.
A depth buffer stores how far away every pixel is, so nearer surfaces hide farther ones.
Gouraud shading, from Henri Gouraud's 1971 paper, lights the corners of each triangle and blends between them, so a sphere looks round instead of faceted.
Textures are pictures wrapped onto triangles.
Getting the perspective right meant a division at every pixel, and a division was slow.
One programmer who wrote about it at the time found that dropping the division made his texture mapper seven times faster, and made the picture look wrong.
Real models load from the period files: a globe with its map, and a car made of twelve parts.
On the 1998 code, built as 32-bit, all twenty-one rungs pass, and the engine's own software renderer draws a lit sphere.
A textured frame from that path is not working yet, and we do not claim it.
On BRender 1.4, the modern fork kept by Zane van Iperen, erysdren and contributors, the same twenty-one rungs pass in 64-bit.
You can open the 1998 sample models in a viewer on a modern PC today, and play a short game built on the same engine.
One thing to keep: rebuild in steps you can check, and a failure tells you where to look.
The voice you heard is a synthesized version of mine.
Every number on screen links to its source under the video.
